chief_complaint: severe dry eyes and dry mouth with bilateral salivary gland enlargement
hpi_details: 50F presenting with several months of severe dry eyes and dry mouth, with recent bilateral parotid gland swelling.
ideas: She thinks her dryness is an extreme symptom of menopause and that her swollen cheeks are caused by blocked salivary ducts from dehydration.
concerns: She is worried that the lumps along both sides of her jaw are malignant salivary gland tumors.
expectations: She hopes to get prescription moisturizing drops for her eyes and mouth, and an ultrasound to check the swelling in her cheeks.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Sjögren Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes objective dry-eye/salivary testing and serology for diagnosis, symptomatic sicca management, and lymphoma surveillance for gland swelling, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe dry eyes and dry mouth with bilateral salivary gland enlargement
Key HPI features: 50F presenting with several months of severe dry eyes and dry mouth, with recent bilateral parotid gland swelling.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Bilateral, mildly enlarged, soft, non-tender parotid glands, symmetric. Conjunctival injection with reduced tear meniscus. Dry, fissured oral mucosa with dental caries. No cervical lymphadenopathy or firm/asymmetric gland masses. Joint exam without synovitis.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Sjögren Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Age-related dry eyes/mouth without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Firm, asymmetric, or rapidly enlarging gland swelling — raises concern for lymphoma, a known complication.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with objective dry eye testing (Schirmer test/ocular staining), salivary flow measurement, and anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB serology; consider minor salivary gland biopsy if serology is negative but suspicion remains high

Manage symptomatically: artificial tears/punctal plugs for dry eyes, saliva substitutes and dental care for dry mouth, with a secretagogue (pilocarpine or cevimeline) considered for significant symptoms after contraindication review
Monitor for lymphoma risk: any firm, asymmetric, or rapidly enlarging gland swelling requires urgent imaging and biopsy
Screen for extraglandular involvement (arthralgia, Raynaud's, peripheral neuropathy, renal tubular acidosis) and refer to rheumatology for ongoing management.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Clinical Guidance

reference_soap.subjective: 50F presenting with several months of severe dry eyes and dry mouth, with recent bilateral parotid gland swelling.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Bilateral, mildly enlarged, soft, non-tender parotid glands, symmetric. Conjunctival injection with reduced tear meniscus. Dry, fissured oral mucosa with dental caries. No cervical lymphadenopathy or firm/asymmetric gland masses.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation (severe xerostomia/xerophthalmia with bilateral parotid enlargement) suggestive of primary Sjögren syndrome; confirmatory Schirmer test and anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB serology pending.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm with Schirmer test, salivary flow measurement, and anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB serology, with minor salivary gland biopsy if serology is negative but suspicion remains high. Begin symptomatic sicca management and monitor gland swelling closely, escalating urgently for any firm, asymmetric, or rapidly enlarging swelling. Screen for extraglandular involvement and refer to rheumatology.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Sjögren Syndrome Primary Autoimmune Exocrinopathy
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for severe dry eyes and dry mouth with bilateral salivary gland enlargement
Select appropriate confirmatory testing (Schirmer test, salivary flow, anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB) for suspected Sjögren syndrome
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune exocrinopathy in which lymphocytes infiltrate and destroy the lacrimal and salivary glands, causing severe dry eyes and dry mouth, confirmed by anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies.
red_flags: Firm, asymmetric, or rapidly enlarging gland swelling — raises concern for lymphoma, a known complication

must_ask.say: How severe is the dryness — do you need to sip water constantly, or use eye drops often?
How long have you had this dryness?
Have your glands in front of your ears been swollen?
Have you had more cavities than usual because of the dry mouth?

history.answer: Doctor, my eyes and mouth have become unbearably dry over the past few months, and recently both sides of my cheeks started swelling up.
The dryness began gradually around six months ago and steadily worsened, while the puffiness in my cheeks developed about three weeks ago.
The dryness affects both eyes and my entire mouth, and the swelling is right in front of both ears along the jawline.
My eyes feel constantly gritty, like there is sand inside, and they burn and turn red. I can barely produce any tears even if I try to cry.
My mouth is completely parched and feels like cotton. I have to sip water constantly just to talk or swallow dry food like bread and crackers.
About three weeks ago, both sides of my face puffed up softly. They are not painful, rock-hard, or hot, just swollen on both sides.
Yes, my dentist recently found several new cavities despite my regular brushing, and my gums have been feeling irritated.
Wind, dry indoor air, and air conditioning make my eye burning worse. Drinking water temporarily wets my mouth, but the dryness returns immediately.
I have tried over-the-counter artificial eye drops and keeping a water bottle with me everywhere, but they only give a few minutes of relief.
No, I have never had severe dryness or facial swelling like this before in my life.
I do not have any joint pain, morning stiffness, or facial rashes. My skin feels somewhat drier than usual, but nothing severe.
No, my fingers do not change color to white or blue when I am cold.
I have had no fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss. The swelling has not grown rapidly or become hard.
No numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, or dizziness. My vision gets slightly blurry only when my eyes are severely dry.
I get a slight dry tickle in my throat from the mouth dryness, but I have no cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
No new medications, no sick contacts, no unusual travel, and no toxic chemical exposures at work or at home.
It disrupts my life constantly because I wake up multiple times every night with a dry throat to drink water, and staring at screens at work is very uncomfortable.
I thought all this dryness was just an extreme symptom of menopause and that my swollen cheeks were clogged spit ducts from not drinking enough water.
I'm really worried that these hard swellings on both sides of my jaw might be cancerous tumors.
I'm hoping to get some prescription eye drops and an ultrasound of my cheeks to make sure these swollen glands aren't dangerous.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, hypertension, or thyroid problems.
I had an appendectomy in my twenties without any complications, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I do not take any prescription medications, regular over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements, other than standard artificial tears.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
My mother had rheumatoid arthritis, but there is no family history of lymphoma, cancers, or other autoimmune diseases.
My periods have become irregular over the past year and my last one was four months ago, so I am entering menopause. There is no chance of pregnancy.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine when dining out, perhaps once or twice a month.
I work full-time in an office doing administrative work and live with my husband.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable-appearing woman with bilateral mild facial fullness anterior to the ears, in no acute distress.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 °C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Bilateral conjunctival injection with visibly reduced tear meniscus; sclerae non-icteric.
Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light; extraocular movements intact without nystagmus.
Bilateral mildly enlarged, soft, symmetric, and non-tender parotid glands; dry, dull oral mucosa with a fissured tongue and multiple dental caries; no pus expressed from salivary ducts.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy; no discrete or firm masses.
Normal thyroid gland size and texture; no nodules or tenderness.
Symmetric chest wall expansion with no localized tenderness.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular heart rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Mild generalized cutaneous dryness without rash, purpura, petechiae, or photosensitivity lesions.
No peripheral joint swelling, erythema, warmth, or tenderness; full range of motion preserved in all joints without synovitis.
